topic: The attribution problem in AI agent ROI

tweets.text: Your AI agent did not resolve that ticket by itself. It just happens to get all the credit for it.
tweets.headline: Your agent did not resolve that alone

tweets.text: A customer writes in about a billing error. The agent finds a knowledge base article, drafts a reply. A human steps in and actually fixes the charge. Ticket closes.
tweets.headline: One ticket, four different contributors

tweets.text: Four things touched that ticket. The agent, the knowledge base article, the human who fixed it, and whatever system logged the charge in the first place.
tweets.headline: The agent, the KB, the human, the system

tweets.text: Your ROI dashboard counts all four as one thing. A resolution the agent handled. That is the whole problem in one sentence.
tweets.headline: Dashboards count four contributors as one

tweets.text: Nobody sat down and decided to inflate this number. Most agent platforms were never built to split credit between everyone who touched a ticket.
tweets.headline: Nobody decided to inflate this number

tweets.text: They were built to track one thing: did the conversation end without an escalation. That yes or no quietly becomes "the agent resolved this" on the slide.
tweets.headline: A yes or no becomes agent resolved

tweets.text: Early on this barely matters. The agent is handling simple, self contained requests, so full credit is basically true.
tweets.headline: Full credit used to be roughly true

tweets.text: Then the agent gets wired deeper into the workflow. It pulls from a knowledge base, triggers a macro, hands off mid conversation to a human.
tweets.headline: Then the agent got wired in deeper

tweets.text: More tickets become a team effort. The reporting keeps calling every single one of them a solo win for the agent.
tweets.headline: Every shared win gets called a solo win

tweets.text: Finance rarely catches this by staring at the number. They catch it when two different tools report two different totals for what looks like the same work.
tweets.headline: Finance catches this comparing two totals

tweets.text: Or when someone pulls a sample of agent resolved tickets and finds a human's fingerprints all over half of them. 👀
tweets.headline: A sampled ticket reveals human fingerprints

tweets.text: At that point the conversation is not about how big the savings number is. It is about whether any of the reporting can be trusted at all.
tweets.headline: Now trust is the question, not size

tweets.text: That is a much worse meeting to walk into than one where the savings number just turned out smaller than hoped.
tweets.headline: Trust questions are worse than small numbers

tweets.text: It also wrecks comparisons across teams. A support org with a great knowledge base and tight macros will look like it has a weaker agent than one that lets the agent wing every answer alone.
tweets.headline: This wrecks comparisons across teams too

tweets.text: That is not a difference in agent quality. It is a difference in how generously each team's dashboard hands out credit.
tweets.headline: Not agent quality, just credit generosity

tweets.text: The fix is not a smarter formula bolted onto a bad input. You cannot calculate your way out of a missing record.
tweets.headline: You cannot formula your way out of this

tweets.text: What you actually need is a record of every system and person that touched a ticket, kept at the same level of detail as the resolution itself. 💡
tweets.headline: What is missing is the full record

tweets.text: With that record, credit splits by contribution. The knowledge base article gets a small share. The human who made the fix gets the bigger one. The agent gets exactly what it earned.
tweets.headline: Credit split by actual contribution

tweets.text: Then you can ask the sharper question. Is the agent's independent share actually growing, or is it just riding on better documentation someone else built.
tweets.headline: Ask if the agent's share is really growing

tweets.text: That is the ledger agentworth's audit log keeps by default, tracking every handoff behind a resolution so your ROI number credits what actually happened, not just what closed the ticket.
tweets.headline: The ledger that tracks what actually happened
